young.html: Ten years after the first book, Cervantes wrote a second part. Now something funny has happened: Don Quixote and Sancho are famous. People they meet have read the first book about them! Some laugh at them, some admire them, and a rich Duke and Duchess play tricks on them for fun.

The Duke even makes Sancho governor of an "island" (really a little town). Everyone expects the simple farmer to make a fool of himself. Instead, he solves hard cases so wisely that people are amazed. After ten days, he decides he would rather be free and goes back to his donkey.

young.html: At the very end, Don Quixote comes home, falls ill, and wakes up in his right mind. He is kind, calm and wise, and his friends, especially Sancho, weep for him.

A story inside a story. In Part Two, the characters read about themselves. Write a short story about yourself in which someone hands you a book about... you. What does the book get wrong? What do you do about it?
young.title: Try this: meet your own book

full.text: A book that knows it is a book

full.html: Part Two appeared in 1615, a year before Cervantes died. In its third chapter a student, Sansón Carrasco, tells the knight and squire that the history of their adventures has been printed and read by thousands. From then on, people they meet know them from Part One, and Don Quixote must live up to, and argue with, his own book.

full.name: gb-frames
full.cap: The layers of the story, from you to the knight.

full.html: In 1614, while Cervantes was writing, another author under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda published a false "second part." Cervantes struck back inside the novel: his characters meet a man from the false book, and Don Quixote changes his route from Zaragoza to Barcelona to prove the other book wrong.

The longest episode takes place at the castle of a Duke and Duchess who have read Part One and stage elaborate pranks to make the pair act out their roles. Many readers find these chapters the cruelest in the book: the noble hosts, not the madman, look foolish and unkind.

As a prank, the Duke makes Sancho governor of the "island" of Barataria. Before he leaves, Don Quixote gives him advice on governing: be humble, know yourself, judge with mercy and with care. Sancho, who cannot read, then judges cases with surprising wisdom, for instance finding money hidden in a walking stick, and chooses mercy in a famous puzzle about a bridge and an oath. After ten days of being starved by a doctor and attacked in a staged invasion, he resigns, saying he prefers the freedom of his old life.
In Barcelona, Sansón Carrasco, disguised as the Knight of the White Moon, defeats Don Quixote and makes him promise to go home for a year. At home he falls ill, sleeps, and wakes in his right mind.

full.text: "Good news for you, good sirs, that I am no longer Don Quixote of La Mancha, but Alonso Quixano, whose way of life won for him the name of Good. Now am I the enemy of Amadis of Gaul and of the whole countless troop of his descendants ..."
full.author: Cervantes
full.work: Don Quixote, Part Two, Chapter LXXIV

full.text: "Ah!" said Sancho weeping, "don't die, master, but take my advice and live many years; for the foolishest thing a man can do in this life is to let himself die without rhyme or reason ..."
full.author: Cervantes
full.work: Don Quixote, Part Two, Chapter LXXIV

full.html: Sancho, the realist, now begs his master to ride out again as a shepherd: the squire has caught the dream. The book closes with Cide Hamete's pen, hung up for good, declaring that Don Quixote was born for him alone, "and I for him."

Reading the ending as a simple happy one. Don Quixote's return to sanity is also a kind of loss, and readers have long felt torn: is it wiser to live without illusions, or does something noble die with them?

deep.html: Part Two plays with who is telling the story, who is reading it, and what is "true" in a book. Writers of the last two centuries, from novelists to philosophers, have seen it as the first great novel about the novel itself.

items: What changes when people know your story before they know you?
Is Sancho a good governor because he is simple, or because he has learned from his master?
Is it better to die sane, like Alonso Quixano, or to live with a noble dream?
Who is the real fool in the Duke's castle?

deep.html: Shakespeare died the same spring as Cervantes, in 1616. Both created characters, Falstaff and Sancho, Hamlet and the knight, who seem to step off the page. Later on this ladder, Fielding, Dickens and Dostoevsky (who called Don Quixote the saddest book ever written) all learned from Cervantes.

questions: If you found a book about yourself, what would you hope it said?
Sancho turned out to be a good governor. What makes someone a good leader?
Was it kind or unkind for the Duke and Duchess to play tricks on Don Quixote? Why?
At the end, Sancho wants his master to keep dreaming. Who changed more over the two books, the knight or the squire?
